items.hook: An antibody-drug conjugate more than doubled time without progression in advanced esophageal cancer.

readout.label: Progression hazard ratio vs chemotherapy

items.summary: In a phase 3 trial of 497 patients whose cancer progressed after immunotherapy plus chemotherapy, izalontamab brengitecan beat standard chemotherapy: median progression-free survival was 4.17 vs 1.97 months and median overall survival 9.79 vs 7.20 months. Severe side effects were more common, at 85.1% vs 59.3%. This was an open-label interim analysis at Chinese hospitals only.
items.title: Izalontamab Brengitecan in Recurrent or Metastatic Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma: Research Summary.
items.venue: JAMA

items.hook: A spinal cord atlas finds 111 cell type groups shared across human, macaque and mouse.

readout.label: Cell type groups shared across three species

items.summary: Researchers profiled over one million nuclei from human, macaque and mouse spinal cords using gene expression, chromatin and spatial methods. Cell identity and layout are highly conserved, and the dorsal horn differs most, including a primate-specific glycine receptor subunit switch. The atlas is a descriptive resource, and links to function and disease still need testing.
items.title: A consensus spinal cord cell-type atlas across mouse, macaque, and human.
items.venue: Neuron

items.hook: A SARS-CoV-2 protease triggers sneezing in mice by switching on pain-sensing neurons.
items.summary: The coronavirus protein PLpro directly activated airway pain neurons in mice and in human stem cell-derived neurons, causing sneezing, coughing and pain signals. This needed both PLpro's cutting activity and the TRPA1 ion channel. The work is in mice and cultured cells, so it is unproven that it explains symptoms in people.
items.title: A coronavirus protease activates sensory neurons via TRPA1 to drive sneeze, cough, and pain.
items.venue: Neuron

items.hook: A doped polymer glows over 2000-fold brighter under stress, so afterglow maps hidden strain.
items.hook_turn: so afterglow maps hidden strain.

readout.label: Phosphorescence increase at 160 MPa

items.summary: Chemists found that a phosphorescent probe lights up under pressure when its singlet energy sits within 0.4 eV of the polymer's lowest triplet state. Doped polymers brightened over 2000-fold at 160 MPa, responded from about 2 MPa, and survived 500 pressure cycles. The rule is empirical, drawn from a set of probes, and tested in the lab only.
items.title: Molecular Mechanophores Based on Stress-Enhanced Exciton Transition between Phosphorescent Probes and Polymer Matrix
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: An engineered thiamine enzyme joins two molecules into rings, a first for its enzyme class.

readout.label: Top enantiomeric excess of ring products

items.summary: Researchers mined a new thiamine diphosphate-dependent enzyme and engineered a variant (F484S) that performs an intermolecular [3 + 2] annulation, building chiral spirooxindole lactones. It handled 30 substrate pairs with up to 99% ee and scaled to 2 mmol. The reaction covers one product family, and larger scale is untested.
items.title: Reprogramming ThDP-Dependent Enzyme for Intermolecular [3 + 2] Annulation via a Homoenolate Intermediate
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: Visible light and acetaldehyde turn nitrogen in air into nitric acid at 200 C and low pressure.

readout.label: Nitric acid formation rate from air

items.summary: Acetaldehyde oxidizes to peracetic acid over stainless steel, and light turns that into radicals that oxidize N2 to nitric acid at 1 to 5 bar. The authors report 110.8 umol per hour and 0.45% N2 conversion, far above earlier systems. Yields are lab scale, conversion is low, and energy cost versus current industry is not shown.
items.title: Acetaldehyde-Mediated Direct Conversion of Air to Nitric Acid
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: A molybdenum enzyme passes sulfur over 50 angstroms along a persulfide relay to make ergothioneine.

readout.label: Sulfur transfer distance between active sites

items.summary: Using cryo-EM, crystallography and spectroscopy, the team showed how a bacterial enzyme pulls sulfur from cysteine and relays it to a molybdenum center to attach it to a histidine derivative. The reaction is reversible, hinting ergothioneine stores oxidizing power. Findings come from one enzyme in one bacterium, and the metabolic role is inferred.
items.title: A Molybdoenzyme Mediates Carbon–Sulfur Bond Making and Breaking in Ergothioneine Biosynthesis
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: A new mass spectrometry method separates fatty acid double-bond position and geometry in bacteria.
items.summary: A chemical derivatization that preserves stereochemistry, paired with ion mobility mass spectrometry, resolves both where double bonds sit and whether they are cis or trans. It revealed dose-dependent antibiotic adaptation in Pseudomonas aeruginosa and mapped lipid isomers in mixed colonies. The biological interpretations are suggestive and come from a few bacterial species in culture.
items.title: Anti -Dihydroxylation-Enabled Dual-Resolution Profiling and Imaging of Fatty Acid C═C Bond Isomers
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: A cage molecule binds iodide in water as strongly as biological binders, excluding other halides.

readout.label: Iodide binding constant in water

items.summary: Chemists built an organic cage with halogen- and hydrogen-bond donors. Its halogen-bonding pocket picks out iodide in water with a binding constant of 43,000 per molar, and in DMSO/water it holds iodide plus chloride at once. Results are from NMR titrations of one cage design, not tests in real water samples.
items.title: Simultaneous Selective Recognition of Two Different Anions within a Hydrogen/Halogen-Bonding Cage
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: One water molecule speeds up iodide's reaction with ozone about 23-fold.
items.hook_turn: speeds up iodide's reaction with ozone about 23-fold.

readout.label: Rate boost from one attached water molecule

items.summary: Sea-surface iodide destroys ozone, and a single attached water molecule makes that reaction about 23 times faster. Mass spectrometry of isolated ions, backed by quantum calculations, shows water helps through hydrogen bonding. The measurements are gas-phase ion experiments, so the extrapolation to real seawater and polar air rests on modeling.
items.title: A Single Water Molecule Drives a 20-Fold Acceleration in the Gas-Phase Reaction of Iodide with Ozone
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: A two-solvent electrolyte lets sodium-ion cells run from -50 to 100 C.
items.hook_turn: lets sodium-ion cells run from -50 to 100 C.

readout.label: Pouch cell capacity retention, 300 cycles at 25 C

items.summary: Mixing ethyl propionate with a nonflammable phosphazene solvent weakens how tightly sodium ions are held, so they move faster and form a stable electrode film. Prussian blue and hard carbon cells ran across the wide temperature range, and ampere-hour pouch cells kept 86.3% capacity after 300 cycles. Low-temperature and hot pouch runs lasted only about 100 cycles.
items.title: Hybrid Weakly Coordinated Solvents for Fast-Charging and Wide-Temperature Sodium-Ion Full Batteries
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: An MR contrast agent stays dark until inflamed, scarring tissue switches it on within minutes.
items.hook_turn: until inflamed, scarring tissue switches it on within minutes.
items.summary: The iron-based probe gives almost no MRI signal until oxidation in inflamed tissue turns it on, and it then binds remodeled scar matrix, which boosts and holds the signal. In mouse models of kidney and liver fibrosis it produced disease-linked contrast within minutes of injection. It has been tested only in mice, so human safety and performance are unknown.
items.title: Magnetic Resonance Silent Activatable Probe with Massive Signal Amplification for Rapid Detection of Inflammation-Associated Fibrogenesis
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: Ammonia made during nitrate reduction reshapes the copper catalyst that makes it.
items.hook_turn: reshapes the copper catalyst that makes it.
items.summary: Atomic force microscopy run during the reaction shows copper surfaces change shape in step with whether nitrite or ammonia is the main product. At higher voltage, fast ammonia formation grows copper islands rich in step sites, which the authors explain by copper dissolving and redepositing. The link between surface change and selectivity is a correlation under lab conditions on flat copper.
items.title: Ammonia-Driven Nanoscale Surface Restructuring of Copper Catalysts during Nitrate Reduction Reaction
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: Cold-temperature assembly makes carbon nanospheres with straight radial pores for sodium storage.

readout.label: Capacity retention after 1000 cycles at 2 A g-1

items.summary: Using sheet-like polymer micelles grown at 5 C instead of spherical ones, the team made wrinkled carbon nanospheres about 910 nm wide with 36 nm pores that connect 96% of the way through. As a sodium-ion anode they kept 90.5% capacity after 1000 cycles and beat commercial hard carbon. Tests were on small lab cells.
items.title: Low-Temperature-Mediated Lamellar–Micelle Assembly of Wrinkled Mesoporous Carbon Nanospheres with Aligned Pores and High Interconnectivity
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: A new metal catalyst turns tert-butylacetylene into ring-shaped polymers.
items.hook_turn: into ring-shaped polymers.
items.summary: Ring-shaped polymers lack chain ends and behave differently from linear ones. A new metallacyclobutadiene catalyst, held by two tethers, makes cyclic poly(tert-butylacetylene), which is not typical for this monomer. Evidence for rings comes indirectly from chromatography and viscosity, and the scope so far is preliminary.
items.title: A Double-Tethered Metallacyclobutadiene Catalyst for Cyclic Polymer Synthesis
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: Electrons can act as catalysts that speed up the self-assembly of donor-acceptor complexes.
items.hook_turn: speed up the self-assembly of donor-acceptor complexes.
items.summary: Catalysis normally speeds covalent bond formation. Here a small number of electrons, supplied by electricity, light, or mechanical force, repeatedly speed up the assembly of a donor-acceptor complex, giving near-quantitative yields even in open air. The demonstration covers one type of complex, so generality across other assemblies is still to be shown.
items.title: Electron-Catalyzed Supramolecular Assembly with High Efficiency, Robustness, and Versatility
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: Cheap HFIP solvent can serve as a source of CF3 groups for modifying drug-like molecules.
items.summary: CF3 groups tune how drug candidates behave, and this method pulls them from HFIP, a common cheap solvent, using light, electricity, and an iron catalyst. It adds CF3 to arenes, heteroarenes, and alkenes, and selectively to tryptophan in peptides. Yields and scope are reported for lab-scale reactions only.
items.title: Empowering HFIP as a Radical Trifluoromethylating Reagent by Photoelectrochemical Iron Catalysis
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: Light and chromium catalysis couple allylic alcohols with aldehydes to give any of four stereoisomers.
items.hook_turn: to give any of four stereoisomers.
items.summary: A chromium catalyst, driven by light, couples allylic and propargylic alcohols with aldehydes to make chiral alcohols, including ones with a quaternary carbon. Choosing the alkene geometry and ligand handedness gives any of the four stereoisomers. Computation explains the stereocontrol, but substrates are lab model compounds.
items.title: Photomediated Chromium-Catalyzed Regio-, Diastereo-, and Enantioselective Deoxygenative Coupling of Activated Allylic and Propargylic Alcohols with Aldehydes
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: An electrolyte additive lets a sodium-ion pouch cell reach 200 Wh/kg and keep 162 Wh/kg at -20 C.
items.hook_turn: keep 162 Wh/kg at -20 C.

readout.label: Pouch cell energy density at 25 C

items.summary: A bulky borate additive ties up the PF6 anion, which doubles ionic conductivity from 2.41 to 5.34 mS per cm and lowers the barrier for sodium ions to leave their solvent shell. A 6.8 Ah pouch cell reached 200 Wh per kg at 25 C. The record claim is relative to other sodium-ion cells, and long-term cycling of the pouch cell is not described.
items.title: Solvent/Anion Codepleted Solvation Engineering Enables Low-Coordination Electrolytes for High-Energy and Low-Temperature Sodium-Ion Pouch Cells
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: Embedding LaCl3 nanocrystals keeps a soft solid electrolyte from melting at 150 C.
items.hook_turn: keeps a soft solid electrolyte from melting at 150 C.
items.summary: Amorphous Li-Al-O-Cl electrolytes deform easily but melt when hot. Embedding rigid LaCl3 nanocrystals keeps the material solid at 150 C while conductivity stays above 1 mS per cm. Cells built with it ran stably at 80 C where the base material failed, though only lab-scale cells are described.
items.title: A Crystalline LaCl3 Reinforced Amorphous Oxyhalide Electrolyte for Thermally Stable All-Solid-State Batteries
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: Binding a cofactor to iron cuts the barrier for O2 activation by 12.7 kcal/mol, a 10^10 rate boost.
items.hook_turn: a 10^10 rate boost.

readout.label: Lower barrier for peroxo formation from pterin binding

items.summary: In tryptophan hydroxylase, the pterin cofactor binding to iron lowers the barrier to form the key peroxo intermediate by 12.7 kcal per mol, roughly ten billion times faster. The team used stable nitric oxide as a stand-in for the unobservable oxygen species, read with several spectroscopies. The oxygen result is extrapolated from that analog.
items.title: Role of (Co)substrate Coordination to Iron in Activating Its Two-Electron Reduction of Dioxygen: Mechanism of Pterin Activation in Tryptophan Hydroxylase
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: Deuterium-labeled amino acids let Raman microscopy image protein condensates in live cells without tags.
items.summary: Cells fed deuterated tyrosine and arginine build them into proteins, and stimulated Raman microscopy then shows FUS condensates, linked to ALS, without bulky fluorescent tags. Pulse-chase imaging shows translation stalls in condensates under stress, and tyrosine phosphorylation is seen through a Raman shift. The work is in cultured cells and centers on FUS.
items.title: Specific Amino Acid Imaging of Protein Condensates in Live Cells by Stimulated Raman Scattering Microscopy
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: Phosphorus next to a nickel single-atom catalyst steers deuterium onto haloanilines at chosen sites.
items.summary: Adding phosphorus outside the nickel's main coordination shell lets the catalyst grab the amino group of haloanilines and swap in deuterium from D2O and H2 at specific positions, leaving carbon-halogen bonds intact. A phosphorus-free version is nearly inactive. Evidence is spectroscopy and calculation on a few aniline substrates.
items.title: Functional Specialization of Coordination Spheres Enables Site-Selective Aromatic C–H Isotope Exchange in Ni Single-Atom Catalysts
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: Carbon dots carrying a chiral catalyst drive asymmetric reactions to 93% e.e. and can be reused
items.hook_turn: and can be reused

readout.label: Best enantiomeric excess, aldehyde alkylation

items.summary: Carbon dots with a chiral organocatalyst attached act as both light absorber and handedness controller for making one mirror-image product. They gave up to 84% yield and 93% e.e., were recovered by precipitation and reused five times, and ran in a flow reactor tuned by Bayesian optimization. Only one reaction type (aldehyde alkylation) was tested.
items.title: Conjugate Chiral Carbon Dots for Scalable Asymmetric Photocatalysis in Flow
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: A thin conformal iridium oxide film on TiO2 cuts iridium use by about 84% in water electrolyzers
items.hook_turn: cuts iridium use by about 84% in water electrolyzers

readout.label: Reduction in iridium use vs commercial IrO2

items.summary: Iridium is scarce, and thinning it out usually breaks the electron pathways in the catalyst layer. Here a negatively charged TiOx surface steers iridium into a flat film instead of clumps, keeping conduction intact at 0.166 mg per cm2. Performance matched commercial IrO2, but the abstract reports no long-term durability test.
items.title: Interfacial Confinement Enables Conformal IrOx Nanofilms for Low-Ir-Loading PEM Water Electrolysis
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: A fluorinated COF membrane lets oxygen in and keeps water out, giving lithium-air cells 2700 h of cycling
items.hook_turn: giving lithium-air cells 2700 h of cycling

readout.label: Cycling life in 40% humidity air

items.summary: Water is smaller than oxygen, so size-based filters fail for lithium-air batteries. A membrane with fluorinated chains repels polar water while passing oxygen, supported by molecular dynamics. In 40% humidity air the cell cycled 2700 h, 10.8 times longer than an unprotected one, though this was tested in lab coin-type cells only.
items.title: Breaking the “Micro-Size Inversion” Paradox via a Surface-Chemistry-Driven Molecular Sieving Membrane for Ambient Lithium–Air Batteries
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: A visible-light ring expansion in acridine compounds stores solar energy for up to 1.4 years
items.hook_turn: for up to 1.4 years

readout.label: Maximum energy storage density

items.summary: Molecular solar thermal compounds store sunlight in strained bonds and release it later as heat. These acridine N-oxides absorb blue light at 470 nm, convert to a metastable form, and hold the energy up to 1.4 years in the solid state. Energy density, up to 0.54 MJ/kg, is modest, and the work is on small-molecule chemistry, not devices.
items.title: Visible-Light-Driven Dearomatization via Electrocyclic Ring Expansion for Solar Energy Storage
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: A six-second molecular movie shows disorder spreading through a protein from one broken salt bridge
items.hook_turn: from one broken salt bridge
items.summary: Many proteins switch between folded and floppy states, but the spread of that change is rarely seen. Time-resolved crystallography captured 29 snapshots of a cryptochrome after light exposure, showing disorder start at one broken salt bridge and travel outward like a helix-to-coil change. It covers one protein in crystals, which may constrain motions seen in solution.
items.title: Mapping the Slow Propagation of Disorder across a Photoreceptor’s Tertiary Structure with Time-Resolved Crystallography
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: Defect-rich cerium MOFs use plain oxygen to break down pollutants, holding over 90% BPA removal for 48 h
items.hook_turn: holding over 90% BPA removal for 48 h

readout.label: BPA removal sustained over 48 h

items.summary: Bulky organic linkers were used to create missing-linker defects and oxygen vacancies in a cerium MOF, letting it turn oxygen into superoxide radicals that destroy contaminants without added energy. A membrane flow system kept removal of bisphenol A above 90% for 48 h. Only a few model pollutants were tested, not real wastewater.
items.title: Linker Steric Hindrance-Induced Defect Engineering Enables Oxygen Vacancy-Rich MOFs for Pollutant Degradation
items.venue: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.hook: A high-resolution climate model fixes the bomb cyclone undercount, projecting fewer but wetter, windier storms
items.hook_turn: projecting fewer but wetter, windier storms

readout.label: Projected bomb cyclone rain rise per kelvin

items.summary: Coarse climate models miss about 30% of bomb cyclones, storms that deepen explosively. A 0.25 degree model reduces that bias and projects fewer such storms under strong warming but stronger winds and heavier rain, driven by stronger uplift rather than extra moisture alone. Results come from one model under a high-emissions scenario.
items.title: Improved Simulation and Projection of Northern Hemisphere Bomb Cyclones in a High‐Resolution Coupled Climate Model
items.venue: Geophysical Research Letters

items.hook: Tree rings in eastern China carry a strong El Niño signal in carbon-14 but only a weak solar one
items.hook_turn: but only a weak solar one
items.summary: Carbon-14 in tree rings is mostly used to track the Sun, but data from subtropical Asia are scarce. An annual 1850 to 1933 record from eastern China matches the global calibration curve and shows El Niño years leave a clear imprint, probably through weaker upwelling of carbon-14-poor ocean CO2. It is one site and one tree record.
items.title: Annual Atmospheric Δ 14 C Variations in the Subtropics During 1850–1933 CE Linked to ENSO
items.venue: Geophysical Research Letters

items.hook: A helium fluorescence lidar measures upper-atmosphere temperature at 500 to 700 km altitude
items.hook_turn: at 500 to 700 km altitude
items.summary: Temperatures above about 500 km are hard to measure from the ground. A lidar in Danzhou, China, detects faint fluorescence from metastable helium using a three-wavelength laser and single-photon detectors. Profiles broadly track radar ion temperatures, but the comparison is only qualitative since the instruments measure different quantities.
items.title: Temperature Measurements up to 700 km Using Metastable Helium Fluorescence LiDAR
items.venue: Geophysical Research Letters

items.hook: Cancer cells resistant to PARP inhibitors lean on ISG15, and blocking it restores drug sensitivity
items.hook_turn: and blocking it restores drug sensitivity
items.summary: Drugs called PARP inhibitors work on BRCA1-mutant tumors until resistance appears. In resistant cell lines and patient-derived xenografts, the immune gene ISG15 was turned up and helped cells copy and repair DNA; inhibiting it re-sensitized cells, and TP53BP1 loss also arose. The evidence is from cell and mouse models, not patients.
items.title: ISG15 promotes PARP inhibitor resistance in BRCA1-deficient cells by facilitating DNA replication and repair
items.venue: Nature Communications

items.hook: Mammalian cells that swallowed algae kept over 16 Mb of algal DNA, including chromosomes, for 95 generations
items.hook_turn: kept over 16 Mb of algal DNA, including chromosomes, for 95 generations

readout.label: Algal DNA retained in hybrid cells

items.summary: Gene transfer between distant eukaryotes is thought to be extremely rare. Mammalian cells took up whole algal cells, and some hybrids kept chromosome-scale algal DNA as methylated, silenced domains; cells lacking a DNA methyltransferase retained less. Transfer is far rarer than cell fusion and was shown only in cultured cells.
items.title: Epigenetic gatekeeping enables genome-scale horizontal gene transfer in eukaryotic cells.
items.venue: Nature Communications

items.hook: A reinforcement-learned chest X-ray report model beats prior systems on the ReXrank benchmark
items.hook_turn: beats prior systems on the ReXrank benchmark
items.summary: Models fine-tuned to write radiology reports often generalize poorly across hospitals. This 8-billion-parameter model adds reinforcement learning against rewards for wording, meaning and clinical errors, and scored best on ReXrank with fewer significant errors. Scores are automated metrics plus expert review, not a trial of use in patient care.
items.title: Scaling medical imaging report generation with multimodal reinforcement learning
items.venue: Nature Communications

items.hook: Genomes of five Gulf of Mexico deep-sea species show small populations and declining diversity
items.hook_turn: show small populations and declining diversity
items.summary: The twilight zone of the deep ocean has little conservation data. Genomic samples from 2011 to 2023 gave effective population sizes below viability thresholds, falling diversity in some species, and niche models predicting shrinking habitat. It covers five species in one gulf, so the broader crisis is a possibility rather than shown.
items.title: Extinction risks in deep-sea populations revealed by genomic data and ecological niche modeling.
items.venue: Nature Communications

items.hook: Climate gains for Corn Belt maize shift from southern declines to northern gains near 42°N.
items.hook_turn: from southern declines to northern gains near 42°N.
items.summary: Crop-model runs over 1991 to 2024 in five U.S. states show climate-driven yield contributions turning from negative in the south to positive in the north, tied to the summer warming hole of cooler highs and more rain. In the south, the heat that hybrids need matched the available heat less well over time. The results come from a model, not field trials, so management effects are inferred.
items.title: Latitude modulates climate-driven maize yield gains across the central U.S. “warming hole”
items.venue: Nature Communications

items.hook: Binding a small ligand can push rubisco into new multi-part assemblies, without evolving new protein contacts.
items.hook_turn: without evolving new protein contacts.
items.summary: By sampling more members of one rubisco clade, the authors found a range of oligomeric responses to ligand binding and pinpointed structural features behind the shifts. This suggests ligand binding can open a route to new quaternary structures. The evidence covers one rubisco clade, so how general the route is remains open.
items.title: Structural basis of ligand-mediated transition to higher-order rubisco assemblies
items.venue: Nature Communications

items.hook: A WSe2 photodiode on a lithium niobate chip receives 10 Gbit/s of visible-light data.
items.hook_turn: receives 10 Gbit/s of visible-light data.

readout.label: External quantum efficiency at 638 nm

items.summary: The team built a lateral p-i-n photodiode from tungsten selenide coupled to a thin-film lithium niobate waveguide, using self-aligned doping and defect engineering for good contacts. It reached a 1.12 GHz bandwidth, about 492 mA/W responsivity, and 95.6% quantum efficiency at 638 nm. These are single-device results at one wavelength, so manufacturing yield is untested.
items.title: Thin-film lithium niobate waveguide-integrated p-i-n Tungsten selenide photodiodes with 10Gbit/s data reception
items.venue: Nature Communications

items.hook: Pairing single ruthenium atoms with chromium slows their dissolution 55.7-fold in acidic water splitting.
items.hook_turn: slows their dissolution 55.7-fold in acidic water splitting.

readout.label: Gain in resistance to Ru dissolution vs SACs

items.summary: Atomically dispersed Ru-O-Cr units damp ruthenium oxidation during acidic oxygen evolution, as seen by in situ X-ray absorption. In membrane electrolyzers at 1 A per cm2, degradation was 6.8 times lower than for Ru single-atom catalysts and 14.4 times lower than for commercial RuO2. The authors call it a possible design principle, and long-term durability beyond these tests is not shown.
items.title: Proximal redox coupling enables oxidation damping for stable water electrolysis.
items.venue: Nature Materials
